note: Our own program on a stock C64. No third-party software is involved, so 198x/decisions/capturing-published-software.md does not bite — the glyphs are the machine's character ROM rendering codes we asked it to display.

captures.claim: PETSCII codes and screen codes are different numbers for the same character: the letter A is PETSCII 65 but screen code 1, and screen code 65 is a spade.
captures.why_this_figure: The entry is called a chart and had no chart. Every code the reader might POKE is now visible in one picture, indexed the way they would look it up — row as high nibble, column as low nibble. It also settles the entry's central distinction by showing it rather than asserting it: row 0 begins @ABCDEFG, so A is screen code 1, while the cell at row 4 column 1 (code $41, decimal 65) is a spade.
captures.program: 10 PRINT CHR$(147) / 20 FOR C=0 TO 9:H=48+C:GOSUB 200:NEXT C / 30 FOR C=10 TO 15:H=C-9:GOSUB 200:NEXT C / 70 FOR R=0 TO 15 / 80 FOR C=0 TO 15 / 90 A=1024+(2+R)*40+3+C / 100 POKE A,R*16+C:POKE A+54272,13 / 110 NEXT C:NEXT R / 120 END / 200 POKE 1064+3+C,H:POKE 55336+3+C,1 / 210 POKE 1024+(2+C)*40+1,H:POKE 55296+(2+C)*40+1,1 / 220 RETURN
captures.labels_are_the_machine_s_own: The hex row and column labels are POKEd as screen codes too, not drawn afterwards in an image editor. Everything in the frame came out of the C64, which keeps this a capture rather than an annotated composite.
captures.why_two_loops: The obvious single loop would be FOR C=0 TO 15 with an IF C>9 to switch from digits to letters. That cannot be typed: emu198x#916 — type_string on the C64 silently drops < and > along with # ! % & [ ]. The first attempt entered `(C>9)` as `(C9)`, a legal variable of value 0, so the program ran without error and drew the labels 0123456789:;<=>? instead of 0123456789ABCDEF. Splitting into two loops avoids every dropped character. Verify by comparing the observation's chars_typed against the length of the string: 316 of 316 here.
captures.verification: The caption names the cell at row 4, column 1 as a spade. Checked against the capture by cropping that row and looking, rather than asserted from memory.
captures.post: crop to the 320x200 active area at (48,56) of the 416x312 raster, nearest-neighbour x2

measurements.tested_claim: The entry's Graphics Characters table, which listed e.g. "Spade PETSCII 65, screen code 1" and "Heart PETSCII 83, screen code 19".
measurements.verdict: Every row was wrong, and wrong the same way: it gave the codes for the UNSHIFTED LETTER on that key. 65 and 1 are the letter A; 83 and 19 are the letter S. The spade is PETSCII 97 and screen code 65.
measurements.method: Machine-read rather than derived. PRINT each candidate CHR$ code, then memory_read screen RAM at 1024 and see what landed. No visual identification of glyphs was involved in producing the numbers.

results.solid_block: CHR$(160) -> 96, NOT 160 as the entry had it; screen code 96 renders as a filled block, confirmed by POKEing it and looking

measurements.pattern_found: Screen code = PETSCII - 32 across all thirteen, which corrects the entry's 'Graphics/shifted (varies): check the tables, no simple formula'. There is a formula. The 193-218 range prints the same characters as 97-122, so either appears in listings.
measurements.glyph_names_unchanged: The descriptions — which corner is which, which suit is which — are the entry's own and were not re-derived. Only the two number columns were corrected. The spade was additionally confirmed by eye against the screen-code chart.
gotchas: C64 BASIC accepts 80 characters per typed line. A test line of ten chained CHR$ calls came to about 118 and was silently truncated, so the program never ran and the screen still showed the boot banner. Split long lines.
PRINT output scrolls. Two early reads of screen RAM returned spaces because the rows had moved; dump several rows and find the data rather than trusting a fixed address.
